# Ossie

*Lighthouse Boy*

## Personality

Curious, solemn and full of questions he asks one at a time. He climbs the lighthouse stairs faster than anyone.

## Lore

Ossie is eight years old and lives in the lighthouse on the headland with his grandmother, Ysolde, the Keeper of the Light. He is curious and solemn, with a serious face and a great many questions, which he asks one at a time and waits for properly. He climbs the lighthouse stairs faster than anyone, all one hundred and seventeen of them, and he has counted them more often than he has counted anything else.

### The boy in the tower

Ossie's mother, Morwenna, is a sailor on Captain Annis's Saltlark, and while she is at sea, Ossie lives at the lighthouse with his grandmother. When his mother is home, she lives there too, and sings him to sleep in the little room at the bottom of the tower where she slept as a girl. His father, Tamar, worked in the ropewalk on the Waterfront and died of a fever when Ossie was barely one, so Ossie does not remember him. He has a piece of rope his father made, tied in a knot nobody can name, and he keeps it under his pillow.

Ossie's days have the lighthouse's shape. He helps his grandmother trim the wicks and polish the great lamp in the afternoon, climbs up with her at dusk to light it, and in between he watches the sea. His grandmother counts ships the way other people count sheep, and Ossie has learned to count them with her. She tells him what she thinks of every captain in the harbour, and Ossie writes it all down, though he has been told very firmly not to repeat any of it.

### The logbook

Ossie has decided he will be a lighthouse keeper too. He made the decision last winter, after reading one of his grandmother's old logbooks from cover to cover, and he has already started his own: a little book with a blue cover that Maren the schoolteacher gave him when he told her his plan. In it he writes down every ship that comes in or goes out, with its name, the time and the weather, and every bird he sees, with a drawing. His spelling is improving. His drawings of birds are very good. His drawings of ships are a little like birds.

He walks the long way down to Merchant Street most mornings for Maren's lessons, and he is her most patient pupil, though not her quickest. He asks her one question at a time and does not move on until she has answered it, and some mornings one question is the whole lesson. Lately he has been asking her about the strange things the other children bring in from the beach, and she has started saying she does not know. Ossie writes that down too.

### The entry he does not understand

One night this spring Ossie could not sleep and climbed to the top of the tower by himself. Far out past the headland, under the water, he saw a pale light moving where there should have been nothing. He wrote it in his logbook, with the time and the weather, the way he writes everything. He did not tell his grandmother, because he thought she would send him back to bed, and he did not tell his mother, because she was at sea. He does not know that his grandmother has seen the same lights from the same window on other nights, or that she has not told anyone either.

### What he wants and fears

Ossie wants to keep the light one day, and to see everything first, the way his grandmother does. He is afraid of only one thing, which he has never asked anybody about, one question at a time or otherwise: that one day his mother's ship will not be in his logbook when it should be.

### Hooks

A quest could read Ossie's logbook and find a pattern in it nobody else has noticed, help him climb the tower on a night when the lights come back, or answer one of his questions properly, which is harder than it sounds.
